newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-IMPRESSIVE DAEHLIE DOES IT AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-IMPRESSIVE DAEHLIE DOES IT AGAIN.

text.p: Norway's Bjorn Daehlie lived up to his status as the greatest cross-country skier in history by taking his second gold medal at the Nordic skiing world championships in Tuesday's 15-km freestyle pursuit cross-country race.

Daehlie's win was a confirmation of his superiority as he had built a comfortable lead on his rivals in Monday's first part of the pursuit event, the 10-km classical style, which determined Tuesday's starting order.

Not only did the Norwegian, who set off 28 seconds before Alexei Prokurorov of Russia and 33 seconds before Mika Myllylae of Finland, stay out of reach of his pursuers but he also increased his lead for a winning time of 36 minutes 30.10 seconds.
Interest soon focused on the fierce battle for second place which Myllylae won by outsprinting Prokurorov as they crossed the line over 50 seconds after Daehlie.

Prokurorov was ahead of Myllylae when both men entered the final straight but the Finn, who narrowly avoided falling as he touched the Russian's skis when trying to overtake him, found enough strength to win a close sprint.
By then Daehlie, armed with a Norwegian flag he had picked up as he entered the stadium at the end of the third and final lap, was already enjoying a lap of honour amid the roars of a partisan crowd.
"It's emotional for me to win here in Norway," he explained. "Cross-country means a lot to Norwegians and they are great spectators. The way I behaved at the finish was to thank them."
Myllylae and Prokurorov, who had already lost a further 15 seconds on Daehlie after the first lap, soon realised they would have to fight for second place.
"I started as strong as possible and when I learned that I had gained time after the first few kilometres, I began to think about the gold medal," said Daehlie.
"There was not much we could do against him," said Myllylae. "After what he had done to us yesterday (Monday) I was not expecting miracles.
"I knew my goal would be the silver medal. It was tough but I got it and I'm ever so pleased."

Daehlie, who had already established himself as the king of cross-country skiing before coming to Trondheim by winning six gold medals at world championships, five Olympic titles and a record 33 World Cup wins, will go for more in Friday's relay and in Sunday's grand finale, the 50-km classical style.
"It will not be easy for me in the 50-km and guys like Alexei (Prokurorov) will be very hard to beat," he said. "But I'm feeling really good at the moment and I believe in my chances."
